fields.meta_description: Make a developer landing page for a CLI, SDK, or open-source project, with signup logic and a database behind it. See four examples.
fields.h1: Build a Developer Landing Page That Shows the Code First
fields.hero_description: Get a developer landing page that shows your install command up top and keeps each signup in a database of your own.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds for a Developer Product
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the page an engineer reads, the form they fill in, and the table where every signup waits for a reply.
fields.feature_1:
Your tool, explained the way engineers read

Describe what the product does and the first command a user types. Emergent builds the page around it: a short pitch, the install line, a code sample, and a docs link.
fields.feature_2:
Signup questions that sort by stack

Ask which language and database each visitor uses. The app reads the answers and decides what that person sees next: a Go signup and a Python one get different follow-ups.
fields.feature_3:
Every signup in a database you own

Each waitlist entry, vote, and access request is saved with its answers beside it. Filter by stack or team size to pick who gets invited first, with nothing to export.
fields.feature_4:
Word when a large team asks for access

Pick the requests that matter, such as a team above a size you set, and the app sends a Slack message, email, or in-app alert. A reminder follows if nobody replies to it.
fields.feature_5:
Requests that reach your CRM and tools

The app connects to any tool with an API, HubSpot and Slack among them. An access request arrives in the CRM with its answers attached, and nobody copies rows by hand.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain and the code behind it

Publish on a domain such as get.yourtool.dev; custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits. Paid plans add full code export to your own GitHub repository.

fields.tab_content_1:
On Postgres? 158 of 412 signups get the first invites

Quillrun asks every signup for its hosted beta for a GitHub username and the database they run. Signups on Postgres are tagged for the first invite wave, and everyone else waits for a later one. Of 412 signups in March, 158 run Postgres, Ines Halvorsen among them, and 254 wait for a later wave.
fields.tab_content_2:
Hexley Freight sees its $1,000 monthly price first

A visitor types a monthly call volume into Tessel's SDK page and sees the price at $0.40 per 1,000 calls before signing up. The app saves each estimate with the visitor's email. Marit Solberg at Hexley Freight entered 2,500,000 calls a month and saw a price of $1,000.
fields.tab_content_3:
HubSpot gets every team of 50 or more engineers

Each access request on Corvane's page asks how many engineers will use the platform. Requests from teams of 50 or more engineers are added to HubSpot as deals. In October 14 of 96 requests came from teams that size, Brightwell Labs with 120 engineers among them; the other 82 went to self-serve signup.
fields.tab_content_4:
Which connector is next? Kafka leads with 512 votes

Pell Queue lets visitors vote for the next connector its open-source queue should ship, one vote per GitHub username. The page shows the tally as votes arrive, and contributors can see which connector to pick up. With 1,240 votes in, Kafka has 512, NATS 388, and SQS 340.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Developer Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Seven steps take a developer landing page from its first command to a live page that keeps every signup.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Show a code sample that runs
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Link the docs and the repo
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write the one command a developer runs first, such as the install line, and put it near the top in a block they can copy. Keep it above any feature list.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Put a short code sample under the pitch, 10 lines or fewer, showing the call people make most. Run it against the current release before every publish, and update it when the API changes.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Link the docs and the source repository from the first screen. A developer who wants to read before signing up should never have to hunt for either one.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Choose the single step the page asks for, such as joining a beta or requesting access, and give it one button. Repeat that button lower down instead of adding a second action.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Describe the page in one prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Paste your product description into Emergent with the signup questions you want answered. Emergent builds the page and a table that keeps every answer, ready for a first test.
fields.howto_step_6_des: Decide who answers access requests and how fast. A team that asked for access in the morning should hear from a person the same working day.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Run a test signup yourself and check that the row lands in your table and the alert arrives. Then publish on your own domain (included in Emergent, uses credits) and link it from your README.

faq_plan.q: What is a developer landing page?
faq_plan.a: A developer landing page is a single page that sells a product built for engineers, such as a CLI, an SDK, or a developer platform, and asks for one step. It puts the first command and a code sample near the top, with a link to the docs for readers who want to check the tool before signing up.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a developer landing page?
faq_plan.a: Describe the product and what each signup should tell you in a prompt to Emergent's AI landing page builder. Emergent builds the page and the database its signups fill, and you change any section by prompting. Send a test signup through it, then publish.

faq_plan.q: What should a dev landing page show above the fold?
faq_plan.a: Three things: what the tool does in one line, the command or call that starts it, and the main button. Put a short code sample right under them if it fits on a laptop screen. Leave customer logos and pricing for further down the page.

faq_plan.q: How is a developer landing page different from one for business software?
faq_plan.a: It leads with code instead of screenshots. A crm landing page speaks to a sales lead and asks for a demo. A developer page shows the install line and a working sample, and lets the reader try the tool before talking to anyone. Make the proof different too: point to the changelog and the docs rather than outcome claims.

faq_plan.q: Should a developer landing page include a code sample?
faq_plan.a: Yes, whenever developers call the product from code. Write it in the language your signups use most, and if you support several, add tabs so each reader picks theirs. Give the block a copy button, and fill it with realistic values, such as a real endpoint path and a sample response.

faq_plan.q: Where should a developer landing page link to its documentation?
faq_plan.a: Put it in the top navigation and again beside the main button, labeled plainly as documentation. Link it from the code sample as well, next to the call the sample makes. On Emergent's paid plans, full code export to your GitHub repository lets the page live in the same repo as the docs it links to.

faq_plan.q: Should a developer landing page show pricing?
faq_plan.a: Yes, if the price is public. A saas landing page with seat-based plans can show a plan table; a tool priced by usage should turn a monthly volume into a number, as the SDK example above does. If pricing is set per contract, say so next to the access button instead of hiding it.

faq_plan.q: Should a developer landing page lead with an install command or a signup form?
faq_plan.a: Use the install command when the tool runs locally with no account, and a signup form when it needs an account, a key, or a seat in a hosted beta. Pick one, and keep the other off the first screen. On a page built with Emergent, the data from every signup lives in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: How do I show open-source traction on a developer landing page?
faq_plan.a: Show numbers a developer can check for themselves: contributors, releases this year, and the companies that agreed to be named as users. Link each number to where it lives, such as the repository or the changelog. A page built on Emergent can also show a live count, such as roadmap votes, as they arrive.

faq_plan.q: Where can I find good examples of developer landing pages?
faq_plan.a: Start with the four tabs above: a CLI, an SDK, a developer platform, and an open-source project, each with the rule behind its page. For layouts outside developer tools, the best startup landing pages collection shows how early companies pitch a single product. Copy the structure you like, then write the words for your own readers.

plan.angle: The SERP for developer landing page is mixed: devtools example galleries and template lists (saaslandingpage devtools tag, a Figma developer tool design, a Medium template roundup, related searches for template, examples and html), plus agency pages about hiring a landing page developer and a Reddit thread on tools. The dominant builder intent is a landing page for a developer product: a CLI, an SDK, a developer platform or an open-source project. The top results stop at screenshots. This page shows four working pages built from a prompt, each with the logic behind it: a CLI beta waitlist that sorts signups by database, an SDK page that prices usage before signup, a platform page that sends large teams to sales in HubSpot, and an open-source roadmap vote with a live tally. The FAQ covers the definition, the build, what sits above the fold, how it differs from business software pages, code samples, docs links, pricing, the main button, open-source proof and where to find examples. API landing pages, SaaS pages and startup galleries are siblings and stay out of the headings.

scope.evidence: H1 'Build a Developer Landing Page That Shows the Code First'; hero 'Get a developer landing page that shows your install command up top and keeps each signup in a database of your own.' covers a page for any developer product (CLI, SDK, platform, open source).

intent.evidence: Mixed SERP (devtools galleries, templates, agency pages); writer's call of a landing page for a developer product is the builder intent, delivered with four example tabs, a 7-step how-to and FAQ on above-the-fold, code samples, docs, pricing and examples.

specificity.evidence: Developer vocabulary throughout: 'the install line, a code sample, and a docs link', 'one vote per GitHub username', '$0.40 per 1,000 calls'.

openers.evidence: Paragraphs open on full sentences: 'Describe what the product does...', 'Quillrun asks every signup...', 'Write the one command a developer runs first...'.

craft.evidence: No blocking craft defect; 13 'A, B, and C' lists (QC Q8 P2) recorded as a note.

voice.evidence: Calm, product-led: 'Run a test signup yourself and check that the row lands in your table and the alert arrives.'

truth.evidence: Claims map to claims_used (custom-domain 'included in Emergent and use credits', free-start 'covers building and publishing', code-export 'on paid plans'). No third-party facts or reader-behaviour statistics; reader guidance is phrased as advice ('A developer who wants to read before signing up should never have to hunt for either one'). Tab numbers add up: 158+254=412, 2,500,000/1,000 x $0.40=$1,000, 14+82=96, 512+388+340=1,240. Table from the library (QC V2/V3 pass).

distinct.evidence: D2 hero overlap with coaching-landing-page 23% (under the 30% gate); tabs, how-to and FAQ are developer-specific. 'api landing page' appears in no heading or anywhere on the page; siblings saas/crm/startup appear only as FAQ link anchors.

faq.evidence: 10 on-topic questions, no brand or file-format asks, each answered in its first sentence ('Yes, whenever developers call the product from code.'); hub link in item 2; moat lines in items 6, 8, 9.

images.evidence: Contact sheet matches copy: 'If a signup runs Postgres -> first invite wave', '158 of 412 signups / 254 in a later wave'; '$1,000 for Hexley Freight'; 'Brightwell Labs 120 -> HubSpot deal', '14 of 96 requests / 82 to self-serve'; Kafka 512, NATS 388, SQS 340, 1,240 votes. One hero per tab, readable text.
